The system was designed to incorporate in-situ and continuous acquisition of sample, air and hot-plate temperatures, volumetric flow rate, air humidity, contact pressure, absolute system pressure, and sample live positions to ensure accurate data while minimizing human interference. This is the first experimental setup with such a capability eliminating the shortcomings from prior work. Real-time drying rates, heat and mass transfer coefficients, sample energy absorbed, and input energies were computed, and meaningful correlations were deduced to be used for modeling and simulation work. The conduction and convection heat and mass transfer results were compared against values from other literature experimental studies and were well within the limits of these studies, indicating a high applicability. Independent experimental evaluation of heat and mass transfer correlations for drying of porous materials under relevant conditions also raised important fundamental differences with commonly used conventional flow over flat plate correlations and heat and mass transfer analogies. This is an important consideration for future modeling work on the drying of porous materials. Additionally, the physical properties of the dried paper samples were also evaluated following the TAPPI standards, and these can be compared against other literature studies as well as studying the effect of novel drying methods and the use of auxiliary energies. Experimental investigation of the integration of RF and US energies at varying drying times and sheet moisture conditions during alternating conduction and convection drying (i.e. duplicating commercial multi-cylinder drying) has also been evaluated. 57 DE-EE0009395 The effect of RF integrated with alternating conduction and convection drying was evaluated with varying basis weights and process conditions including varying RF power levels. The results showed that integrating RF drying is indeed an effective method for paper drying applications with greater improvements in drying rates and energy intensities at higher moisture contents. At lower moisture contents, RF is ineffective as a drying method even though the volumetric drying can be used to even out local variations in moisture content profiles (Grassmann 1980). RF drying is especially effective at higher basis weights, as in packaging grades, which are in general more difficult to dry using the current commercial technologies. This analysis complemented theoretical studies on RF’s effects in drying systems. The results demonstrated improvements in drying rate and energy efficiency across a range of RF power levels, paper types, basis weights, and drying approaches, with high repeatability, ensuring a solid foundation for future studies in drying process improvements and simulation-based modeling and commercial implementation. Similar to the RF work, the application of US energy at various frequencies and power levels and at various sheet moisture contents in conjunction with conduction and convection drying was also explored. It is interesting that, for all the basis weights studied, the above regimen of application did not result in any appreciable increase in drying rate improvements or energy intensity improvements when compared to the base case conduction and convection cycles.
